title: Wittgenstein's Tractarian Ontology
description: This work reconstructs the Tractatus as a parameterized model-theoretic system and proves that its central philosophical claims correspond to explicit semantic constraints and provable limits of expressibility.

mathlibDependencies.description: Law of excluded middle (classical logic axiom)

originalContributions: Formal ontology mapping Tractatus propositions to Lean types
Truth-functional compositionality theorem via structural induction
Elementary independence theorem witnessing the Sachverhalt/world correspondence
General WorldModel abstraction with constrained model examples and compatibility lemma
First-order extension using HOAS (higher-order abstract syntax) for quantifier binding
Compositionality extended to first-order propositions with quantifiers
Universal-existential duality and distribution theorems for the extended language
Philosophical annotations bridging formal verification and Wittgensteinian philosophy
Logical-form equivalence (formEq) via Equiv.Perm capturing TLP 4.0141, with rename functor, equivalence relation proofs, and strict three-level hierarchy structEq < formEq < semEq
meta.assumptions: One deliberate axiom: `silence : True` (TLP 7) — a trivially true but axiomatic declaration that enacts Wittgenstein's silence as a formal gesture. All theorems are fully proved with 0 sorries. Uses classical logic (Classical.em) throughout. The companion file TractatusQuantifiers.lean has no sorries or axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) is Wittgenstein's only book-length philosophical work published in his lifetime. It presents a logical atomist ontology: the world consists of facts (obtaining states of affairs), propositions picture possible states of affairs, and all meaningful propositions are truth-functions of elementary propositions. The work culminates in proposition 6.54 — the famous ladder that must be thrown away — and the closing injunction: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.'
overview.problemStatement: This work reconstructs the Tractatus as a parameterized model-theoretic system and proves that its central philosophical claims correspond to explicit semantic constraints and provable limits of expressibility.
overview.proofStrategy: We define types for objects (opaque), states of affairs (abstract), and worlds (predicates on states of affairs). Propositions form an inductive type with elementary, negation, and conjunction constructors. All other connectives are derived. A recursive evaluation function maps propositions to truth values relative to worlds. We then extend to first-order propositions (FOProp) using higher-order abstract syntax (HOAS) for quantifier binding, and prove compositionality, duality, and distribution theorems for the extended language.
keyInsights: The world-as-predicate encoding makes elementary independence trivially true — the assignment IS the world; this is the free model, and constrained models break independence
Truth-functional compositionality follows by structural induction on the proposition type
HOAS encoding of quantifiers allows Lean's structural recursion to handle first-order evaluation without explicit substitution or de Bruijn indices
The formalization necessarily works at the metalevel — we prove theorems ABOUT propositions in Lean, which is precisely the kind of thing Wittgenstein says can only be shown, not said
Classical logic (excluded middle) is used throughout, matching Wittgenstein's bivalent semantics
prerequisites: Familiarity with Lean 4 syntax (inductive types, pattern matching)
Some acquaintance with the Tractatus is helpful but not required

sections.title: Preamble
sections.summary: Module imports, documentation header introducing the formalization scope, and design decisions documenting modeling choices.
sections.mathContext: The preamble imports `Mathlib.Tactic` and opens the `Tractatus` namespace, establishing the classical-logic environment used throughout. It documents the three core design decisions: opaque types for ontological primitives (objects $O$ and states of affairs $S$), worlds encoded as predicates $w : S \to \text{Prop}$, and propositions as an inductive datatype. These choices mirror standard Kripke-style model theory while staying close to Wittgenstein's own picture-theoretic semantics.

sections.title: Objects (TLP 2.02)
sections.summary: Objects as an abstract variable type — simple, structureless entities.
sections.mathContext: Objects are introduced via `variable (O : Type*)`, making $O$ a universally quantified type parameter throughout the file. No structure is imposed on $O$: there are no relations, no equality constraints, no cardinality assumptions. This encodes TLP 2.02 — objects are simple, substance-like entities whose only mathematical role is to serve as arguments in states of affairs.

sections.title: States of Affairs (TLP 2.01)
sections.summary: States of affairs (Sachverhalte) as an abstract type of possible combinations.
sections.mathContext: States of affairs are introduced via `variable (S : Type*)`, a second universally quantified type parameter representing possible combinations of objects (Sachverhalte in TLP 2.01). The type $S$ is left entirely abstract: no combinatorial structure linking $S$ to $O$ is imposed at this level, since the Lean formalization works with the logical space directly. The set of all elements of $S$ forms the logical space $\mathcal{L} = \{s : S\}$ of possible elementary situations.

sections.title: Worlds (TLP 1, 1.1, 2.04)
sections.summary: Worlds as predicates determining which states of affairs obtain.
sections.mathContext: A world is defined as `def World (S : Type*) := S → Prop`, i.e., a predicate $w : S \to \text{Prop}$ that selects which states of affairs obtain. This encodes TLP 1 ('The world is everything that is the case') and TLP 2.04 ('The totality of obtaining states of affairs is the world'). The actual world is one such predicate; the logical space is the powerset $\mathcal{P}(S)$, each element being a possible world.

sections.title: Independence Structure (TLP 2.061-2.062)
sections.summary: IndependentWorlds typeclass and its default instance for the free Boolean cube.
sections.mathContext: The `IndependentWorlds` typeclass asserts that for any assignment $f : S \to \text{Prop}$ there exists a world $w : S \to \text{Prop}$ such that $\forall s,\, w(s) \leftrightarrow f(s)$. This encodes TLP 2.061–2.062: states of affairs are independent of one another, so any combination can obtain. The default instance for `World S` is trivial — the assignment itself IS the world — giving the free Boolean cube $\{0,1\}^S$ as the canonical model of full independence.

sections.title: Propositions (TLP 4.21, 5)
sections.summary: Inductive type for propositions: elementary, negation, conjunction.
sections.mathContext: Propositions form an inductive type `Proposition S` with three constructors: `elementary : S → Proposition S` (atomic propositions picturing single states of affairs), `neg : Proposition S → Proposition S` (negation), and `conj : Proposition S → Proposition S → Proposition S` (conjunction). This is the minimal truth-functional basis consistent with TLP 4.21 and TLP 5: all other connectives are defined terms, and every proposition is ultimately a truth-function of elementaries.

sections.title: Derived Connectives (TLP 5.101)
sections.summary: Disjunction, implication, biconditional, and NAND defined from negation and conjunction.
sections.mathContext:
The four derived connectives are: $p \lor q := 
eg(
eg p \land 
eg q)$ (De Morgan disjunction), $p 	o q := 
eg p \lor q$ (material conditional), $p \leftrightarrow q := (p 	o q) \land (q 	o p)$ (biconditional), and $p \mid q := 
eg(p \land q)$ (Sheffer NAND). These definitions implement TLP 5.101's truth-table analysis and TLP 5.5's claim that all truth-functions arise from a single binary operation. No new constructors are added to the inductive type; the derivations are purely definitional.

sections.title: Semantic Evaluation (TLP 2.21, 4.06)
sections.summary: Recursive truth-value evaluation of propositions relative to worlds, including Bool-valued evaluator and correctness bridge theorem.
sections.mathContext: The function `eval : Proposition S → World S → Prop` is defined by structural recursion: `(elementary s).eval w = w s`, `(neg p).eval w = ¬ p.eval w`, `(conj p q).eval w = p.eval w ∧ q.eval w`. A parallel Bool-valued evaluator `evalB : Proposition S → World S → Bool` uses `decide` to return decidable truth values. The bridge theorem `evalB_correct` proves `evalB p w = true ↔ eval p w`, connecting the computational and propositional semantics.

sections.title: Tautology and Contradiction (TLP 4.46, 6.1)
sections.summary: Definitions of tautology (true in all worlds), contradiction (false in all worlds), and nontrivial propositions.
sections.mathContext: `IsTautology p` is defined as `∀ w : World S, p.eval w` and `IsContradiction p` as `∀ w : World S, ¬ p.eval w`. A proposition is `IsNontrivial` if it is neither a tautology nor a contradiction — i.e., it has at least one verifying world and at least one falsifying world. These definitions formalize TLP 4.46 ('The simplest cases of tautology are...') and TLP 6.1 ('The propositions of logic are tautologies').

sections.title: General World Models
sections.summary: WorldModel structure parameterizing semantics over arbitrary world collections. Includes freeModel, evalM, IsTautologyM, IsContradictionM, generalized compositionality (main result), and a compatibility lemma proving evalM over freeModel equals the original eval.
sections.mathContext: A `WorldModel S` is a structure `⟨W, holds⟩` where `W : Type*` is the world carrier and `holds : W → S → Prop` is the satisfaction relation, abstracting $\models$ from any fixed representation. The free model `freeModel S : WorldModel S` sets `W = World S` and `holds w s = w s`. The generalized evaluator `evalM M p w` recurses on `Proposition S` using `M.holds`, and `truth_functional_compositionality_gen` proves that worlds indistinguishable on atomics evaluate all compounds identically — the main result for arbitrary $M$.

sections.title: Main Theorems
sections.summary: Core theorems 1-13: compositionality (main result), independence, bivalence, connective semantics, and NAND functional completeness.
sections.mathContext: The thirteen main theorems cover: (1) `truth_functional_compositionality` — if $w_1$ and $w_2$ agree on all $s : S$ then $p.\text{eval}\, w_1 \leftrightarrow p.\text{eval}\, w_2$; (2) `elementary_independence` — for any $f : S \to \text{Prop}$ there exists $w$ with $w(s) \leftrightarrow f(s)$; (3) `bivalence` — $p.\text{eval}\, w \lor \neg p.\text{eval}\, w$ for all $w$; through (13) `nand_functional_completeness` — every truth-function expressible by `neg`/`conj` is also expressible using only NAND ($\uparrow$), formalizing TLP 5.5. The section also proves classical tautologies including $p \lor \neg p$ and De Morgan laws.

sections.title: Constrained World Models
sections.summary: Abstract constrained model (ConstrainedWorld with constrained_independence_fails, main result) and concrete weather model (WeatherFacts with weather_independence_fails). Both demonstrate that independence is a modeling choice, not a logical law.
sections.mathContext: `ConstrainedWorld S a b` is a subtype `{w : World S // w a → w b}` imposing the constraint that state $a$ obtaining forces state $b$ to obtain. The theorem `constrained_independence_fails` proves $\neg \forall f : S \to \text{Prop},\, \exists cw : \text{ConstrainedWorld}\, S\, a\, b,\, \forall s,\, cw(s) \leftrightarrow f(s)$ — no world in the constrained model can make $a$ true and $b$ false. The weather model concretizes this with `WeatherFacts = {rain, clouds}` and the constraint `rain → clouds`, proving `weather_independence_fails`.

sections.title: Concrete Examples
sections.summary: TwoFacts instantiation with rain/snow, Prop-valued and Bool-valued evaluation examples.
sections.mathContext: `TwoFacts` is an inductive type with constructors `rain` and `snow`, giving a two-element type $S = \{\text{rain}, \text{snow}\}$ that concretely inhabits the abstract $S$ parameter. Example worlds are defined by specifying which subset of `{rain, snow}` obtains, and specific propositions such as `elementary .rain` and `conj (elementary .rain) (elementary .snow)` are evaluated both with `eval` (Prop-valued) and `evalB` (Bool-valued), illustrating the bridge theorem with ground-level computations.

sections.title: Structural vs Semantic Equivalence (TLP 4.0141)
sections.summary: Defines structural (structEq), semantic (semEq), and logical-form (formEq via Equiv.Perm) equivalence. Proves formEq is an equivalence relation, establishes strict hierarchy structEq < formEq < semEq, and proves the divergence theorem structEq_ne_semEq (main result).
sections.mathContext: Three equivalence relations are defined on `Proposition S`: `structEq` (syntactic identity up to the inductive tree), `semEq p q` ($\forall w,\, p.\text{eval}\,w \leftrightarrow q.\text{eval}\,w$, truth-table equality), and `formEq p q` ($\exists \sigma : \text{Equiv.Perm}\, S,\, \forall w,\, p.\text{eval}\,w \leftrightarrow q.\text{eval}\,(w \circ \sigma)$, isomorphism of truth-table patterns). The strict hierarchy $\text{structEq} \subsetneq \text{formEq} \subsetneq \text{semEq}$ is witnessed by: `elementary .rain` vs `elementary .snow` (formEq but not structEq) and `neg (neg (elementary s))` vs `elementary s` (semEq but not formEq), formalizing TLP 4.0141.

sections.title: The expresses Relation and Analytical Decomposition
sections.summary: The expresses relation (TLP 4.12) bridging object and meta language, and a three-way classification of all results: core invariants, model assumptions, and formal limits.
sections.mathContext: The `expresses` relation is defined as `expresses p w ↔ p.eval w`, connecting a proposition $p$ to the worlds in which it holds — the formal correlate of TLP 4.12 ('A proposition shows how things stand if it is true'). A three-way classification partitions all proved results: (1) core invariants (compositionality, independence, bivalence) that hold in the free model; (2) model assumptions (independence failure in constrained models) that are contingent on the choice of $W$; and (3) formal limits (the silence theorem, the limits of expressibility) that hold at the meta-level about what `expresses` can and cannot capture.

sections.title: The Limits of Formalization (TLP 6.54, 7)
sections.summary: World-constant triviality lemma, saying/showing triviality theorem, contingent propositions theorem, nontrivial predicate theorems, proposition seven, nontrivial expressibility theorems, the ladder of TLP 6.54, and the axiom of silence.
sections.mathContext: The silence theorem proves that any proposition constant across all worlds — i.e., $\forall w_1 w_2,\, p.\text{eval}\,w_1 \leftrightarrow p.\text{eval}\,w_2$ — is either a tautology or a contradiction, never genuinely contingent. The `saying_showing_triviality` theorem formalizes that truth-functional propositions cannot express the structural features they show (TLP 4.1212). The section culminates in `axiom silence : True` — a deliberate Lean `axiom` declaration encoding TLP 7 ('Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent') as a formal gesture: axiomatic, trivially true, yet irreducible to any proof.

conclusion.summary: We have formalized the ontological skeleton of the Tractatus: objects, states of affairs, worlds, and truth-functional propositions. Thirty-seven theorems and lemmas are fully proved with 0 sorries, covering compositionality, independence, bivalence, connective semantics, functional completeness, constrained model independence failure, saying/showing triviality, structural vs semantic equivalence, and the three-level equivalence hierarchy structEq < formEq < semEq. The silence of Proposition 7 is enacted via a deliberate axiom.
conclusion.implications: This demonstrates that the formal core of the Tractatus — often dismissed as merely philosophical rather than mathematical — admits precise statement and machine-verified proof. The exercise also reveals where formalization reaches its limits: the saying/showing distinction, the nature of logical form, and the self-undermining character of 6.54 all resist capture in any formal system.
openQuestions: Could dependent types better capture TLP 2.0141 — that an object's form IS its combinatorial possibility?
Is there a formalization that captures the saying/showing distinction without collapsing it?
How does this propositional framework relate to Wittgenstein's later rejection of logical atomism?
Can the N-operator connection (TLP 5.52) be made precise for infinite domains, or is Geach (1981) correct that it fails?
Does the HOAS encoding faithfully capture the Tractarian view of variables, or does it import too much metatheory?

What is the right spectrum of world models between the free model (full independence) and highly constrained physical models? Can an IndependentWorlds typeclass characterize exactly which models satisfy elementary independence?

references.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.note: Translated by C.K. Ogden and F.P. Ramsey. The numbering system (1, 1.1, 2.01, etc.) indicates logical dependencies between propositions.

references.title: Introduction to the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
references.note: Russell's introduction — which Wittgenstein reportedly disliked — interprets the Tractatus within the framework of Principia Mathematica.

references.title: A set of five independent postulates for Boolean algebras
references.venue: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 14
references.note: Introduces the Sheffer stroke (NAND), which Wittgenstein references in TLP 5.5 as showing all truth-functions reduce to a single operation.

references.title: Wittgenstein's Operator N
references.note: Argues that Wittgenstein's N-operator cannot handle all quantified propositions as claimed in TLP 5.52, particularly for infinite domains.

references.title: Generality, Truth-Functions, and Expressive Capacity in the Tractatus
references.note: Shows that the claim that all propositions are truth-functions of elementary propositions (TLP 5) is undermined by the infinite-domain case of quantification.

additionalFiles.description: First-order extension: FOProp type with HOAS quantifiers, evaluation, compositionality, duality, and distribution theorems (TLP 5.52, 5.521, 5.526)

mainTheorems.name: tautology_is_world_invariant
mainTheorems.description: A proposition is a tautology iff it holds in every world (TLP 6.1)
mainTheorems.leanType: (∀ w : World S, p.eval w) ↔ IsTautology p

mainTheorems.name: truth_functional_compositionality
mainTheorems.description: Worlds agreeing on elementaries agree on all compounds (TLP 5)
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (p : Proposition S) (w₁ w₂ : World S), (∀ s, w₁ s ↔ w₂ s) → (p.eval w₁ ↔ p.eval w₂)

mainTheorems.name: elementary_independence
mainTheorems.description: Any truth-value assignment to states of affairs is realizable (TLP 2.061)
mainTheorems.leanType: ∃ w : World S, ∀ s : S, w s ↔ assignment s

mainTheorems.name: excluded_middle_tautology
mainTheorems.description: p ∨ ¬p is a tautology — paradigmatic logical truth (TLP 4.46)

mainTheorems.name: truth_functional_compositionality_fo
mainTheorems.description: Worlds agreeing on elementaries agree on all first-order compounds including quantifiers (TLP 5, extended)
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (p : FOProp S D) (w₁ w₂ : World S), (∀ s, w₁ s ↔ w₂ s) → (p.eval w₁ ↔ p.eval w₂)

mainTheorems.name: forall_exists_duality
mainTheorems.leanType: (FOProp.negFO (FOProp.forall_ (fun d => FOProp.negFO (f d)))).eval w ↔ (FOProp.exists_ f).eval w

mainTheorems.name: forall_distrib_conj
mainTheorems.leanType: (FOProp.forall_ (fun d => FOProp.conjFO (f d) (g d))).eval w ↔ (FOProp.conjFO (FOProp.forall_ f) (FOProp.forall_ g)).eval w

mainTheorems.name: truth_functional_compositionality_gen
mainTheorems.description: Compositionality generalized to arbitrary world models (not just the free model)
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (M : WorldModel S) (p : Proposition S) (w₁ w₂ : M.W), (∀ s, M.holds w₁ s ↔ M.holds w₂ s) → (evalM M p w₁ ↔ evalM M p w₂)

mainTheorems.name: evalM_free_eq_eval
mainTheorems.description: Compatibility: evalM over freeModel equals the original eval
mainTheorems.leanType: evalM (freeModel S) p w = p.eval w

mainTheorems.name: weather_independence_fails
mainTheorems.description: Elementary independence fails in the constrained weather model — rain without clouds is impossible

mainTheorems.name: formEq_implies_truth_table_iso
mainTheorems.description: Logical-form equivalence implies truth-table isomorphism via world relabeling
mainTheorems.leanType: p.formEq q → ∃ f : World S → World S, ∀ w, p.eval w ↔ q.eval (f w)

mainTheorems.name: formEq_not_structEq_witness
mainTheorems.description: Strict separation: atom-swapped elementaries are formEq but not structEq

mainTheorems.name: semEq_not_formEq_witness
mainTheorems.description: Strict separation: double-negated elementary is semEq but not formEq to elementary

mainTheorems.name: constrained_independence_fails
mainTheorems.description: Independence fails in constrained models — it is a modeling choice, not a logical law (TLP 2.061 contrast)
mainTheorems.leanType: ¬ ∀ assignment : S → Prop, ∃ cw : ConstrainedWorld S a b, ∀ s, cw.val s ↔ assignment s

mainTheorems.name: structEq_ne_semEq
mainTheorems.description: Structural and semantic equivalence diverge: truth conditions cannot capture logical form (TLP 4.0141)
mainTheorems.leanType: ∃ (p q : Proposition S), Proposition.semEq p q ∧ ¬ Proposition.structEq p q
